title: Life cycles of plants and animals
summary: Second graders observe a bean plant, a butterfly and a frog grow and change, put each life cycle in order, and discover what all living things share.
brief: Life cycles of plants and animals for grade 2 science: a two-week unit of ten 40-minute lessons. Students observe and compare the life cycles of a bean plant, a butterfly and a frog, put the stages in order, and notice what all living things share: they are born, grow, reproduce and die. Start a bean-sprouting observation in the first lesson that students record in an observation journal through the unit, use picture cards for sequencing, and read aloud a picture book where it helps. Short check-ins along the way are practice and are not graded. The only graded work is the final drawing-and-labeling assessment of one life cycle, done in the last lesson and scored with a simple rubric: it is 100% of the unit grade.
policies:
Observation journals, check-ins and quizzes are practice and are not graded. The final life cycle drawing is scored with the rubric; a student who is absent draws it on their return.

Spelling does not count toward the score: a name that can be read, such as "krisalis", is accepted. Read any prompt aloud for a student who needs it.

Beans and other materials are for looking at, never for eating. Tell me about any food allergies before the unit begins, especially to beans, peas or peanuts, which are all legumes.

l_cefbb6b58ef7.title: What is a life cycle?
l_cefbb6b58ef7.summary: Students learn that living things are born, grow, reproduce and die, and plant bean seeds to observe in a journal.

segments.title: Then and now
segments.description:
Show two photos of the same cat, one as a tiny kitten and one as a grown cat.
Ask, “What do you notice? How did this cat change?”
Students turn to a partner and share one change, such as size, fur or what it can do.
Collect a few answers on the board under the heading “Changes”.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect: bigger, taller, stronger, eats different food. Accept any real change. Bring two cat photos, or use any pet students know. Do not correct answers yet. Next you name these changes a life cycle.

segments.title: Born, grow, reproduce, die
segments.description:
Say, “All these changes together are a life cycle.”
Use the cat to teach four words with a hand motion each: born, grow, reproduce (have young), die.
Draw a circle showing kitten → adult cat → new kittens. Explain that the new kittens grow up and can have kittens of their own. Each cat’s life ends when it dies.
Students say each word and do the motion with you.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep the talk about death gentle and matter-of-fact: it happens to every living thing, and the young carry on the cycle. Some students may have lost a pet or relative, so stay calm and brief. Common mistake: thinking a life cycle is only growing up.

segments.title: Put the chicken in order
segments.description:
Give each pair a set of four picture cards showing a chicken’s life.
Pairs put the cards in order and say the story of the chicken to each other.
Then the class checks the order together and uses the words born, grow and reproduce.
Point out that the last card leads back to the first.
segments.teacherNotes:
This is practice, not graded. Cards, in the expected order:
1. An egg in a nest (a chick develops inside).
2. A fluffy chick (the chick hatches, then grows).
3. A full-grown hen (grown up).
4. A hen sitting on new eggs (reproduce, and the cycle starts again).
Common mistake: putting the hen before the chick. Ask, “Which one came from the egg?” Print or draw the card sets ahead, plus extra sets for absent students.

segments.title: Plant a bean and start the journal
segments.description:
Show how to plant: place a soaked bean seed in a clear zip bag with a damp paper towel, then seal it.
Each student plants one seed and writes a name on the bag. Tape the bags to a window that does not get direct sun, or set them on a bright shelf near it. Direct sun overheats sealed bags and makes them mold.
Students open their observation journal and write the date on page one.
They draw their seed with colored pencils and label it “seed”.
Explain that we will draw the same seed again as it changes, because we will watch this bean all unit.
segments.teacherNotes: Prep: use dry pinto or lima beans from the grocery store. Soak them in water 8 to 12 hours the night before; have spares. Safety: raw dry beans are harmful to eat (raw lima and kidney beans can make people sick), beans are a choking hazard, and some students have legume allergies, so check records. Seeds are never eaten and hands stay out of mouths. Wash hands after planting. Keep bags sealed; a moldy bag is thrown away by the teacher. Sprouts need several days, so today’s entry is only the seed.

segments.title: What is a life cycle?
segments.description:
Gather students on the rug with their journals.
Ask each pair to finish this sentence: “A life cycle is...”
Have a few pairs share, then say the four words together one more time with the motions.
Tell students that they will check their bean seed again soon to see if it has changed.
segments.teacherNotes: Good answers: the changes a living thing goes through; born, grow, reproduce, die. If a student says only “growing”, add the other words. Listen for who can use the four words, and note students to support later. Not graded.

keyIdeas: A life cycle is the set of changes a living thing goes through during its life.
Every living thing is born, grows, reproduces and dies.
The stages of a life cycle happen in a fixed order, and the cycle starts again with the new young.
Scientists learn about life cycles by observing closely and recording what they see, so we plant bean seeds and draw them in a journal.

When a living thing begins its life.
To get bigger and change.
To make young that are like the parent.
The small part of a plant that can grow into a new plant.
To look closely and notice details.

study.overview: Today you learned that every living thing has a life cycle. A life cycle is the set of changes a living thing goes through during its life. You looked at a cat, put a chicken’s life in order, and planted a bean seed to watch in your journal. Scientists learn by looking closely and writing down what they see, and you can do that too.

points.heading: A life cycle is a set of changes
points.explanation: A life cycle is all the changes a living thing goes through during its life. It is more than just growing up. Think of the cat from class. It began as a tiny kitten. Its size, fur and what it could do all changed. It became a grown cat. Those changes together are the cat’s life cycle.

points.heading: Born, grow, reproduce, die
points.explanation: Every living thing is born, grows, reproduces and dies. Reproduce means to have young. A kitten is born. It grows into an adult cat. The adult cat can have new kittens. Each cat’s life ends when it dies. Dying happens to every living thing. Try the hand motion for each word at home and say the four words out loud.

points.heading: The stages go in order, and the cycle starts again
points.explanation: The stages of a life cycle happen in a fixed order. The new young begin the cycle again. Remember the chicken cards. First comes an egg in a nest. Next is a fluffy chick. Then comes a full-grown hen. Last, the hen sits on new eggs. Those new eggs lead back to the first card. The hen came from the egg, so the hen cannot come before the chick.

points.heading: Scientists observe and record
points.explanation: Scientists learn about life cycles by looking closely and recording what they see. In class you planted a bean seed in a clear bag with a damp paper towel. You wrote the date in your journal. You drew the seed with colored pencils and labeled it “seed.” Next you will draw the same seed again as it changes. We will watch this bean all unit. Keep the bag sealed and never eat the seed.

l_1de126ec81e2.title: Living and nonliving things
l_1de126ec81e2.summary: Students sort pictures of living and nonliving things and name what living things need to survive.

segments.title: Alive or not alive?
segments.description:
Hold up the photo of the cat from last time and then a photo of a rock.
Ask students to show thumbs up for alive and thumbs down for not alive.
Ask one student to say how they decided.
Say, “Today we find out how to tell.”
segments.teacherNotes: Expect answers like “it moves” or “it breathes.” Accept them. Gently note that a plant does not move much but is still alive. Use this to set up the sort.

segments.title: What living things need
segments.description:
Start a class chart titled “Living things need.”
Use the cat to ask, “What does a cat need to stay alive?” Write food, water and air as students name them.
Show a sunflower photo. Explain that plants need water, air and sunlight to make their own food.
Explain that to survive means to stay alive. Link back to the life cycle: living things are born, grow, reproduce and die, and they need these things along the way.
segments.teacherNotes: Students may add shelter, love or toys. Accept shelter as a real need but keep the chart focused on food, water and air. Rocks do not eat, drink or breathe. Misconception: plants do not eat soil; they make food from sunlight, water and air.

segments.title: Sort the picture cards
segments.description:
Give each pair six picture cards and a two-column mat labeled living and nonliving.
Pairs sort the cards and say one reason for each card to each other.
Walk around and ask, “Does it need food, water and air?”
This is practice and is not graded.
segments.teacherNotes: Cards and answers: cat, living. Rock, nonliving. Bean seed, living. Toy truck, nonliving. Sunflower, living. Plastic ball, nonliving. The bean seed is the tricky card: it looks still but it will grow. Print or draw one card set and one two-column mat per pair ahead of time. Cards only, no real objects needed.

segments.title: Why is a bean seed living?
segments.description:
Bring pairs back together and review the bean seed card.
Ask, “Why did we put a bean seed in the living group?”
Ask which needs our planted bean is getting: water from the damp paper towel and air in the bag.
Explain that a bean seed has food stored inside it to help it begin growing. Add a drawing of a bean next to each need on the chart, labeling its food as stored inside the seed.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: it will grow into a plant, it needs water. A toy truck can move but does not grow or need food, so it stays nonliving. Dry seeds are dormant, not dead: they wake up when they get water.

segments.title: Check the bean bags
segments.description:
Each student gets their sealed bag from the window spot (out of direct sun) and looks closely without opening it.
Students look for changes in the bean and the paper towel.
In their journal they draw what they see and write one word, such as wet, bigger or root.
Return the bags to the window.
segments.teacherNotes: Seeds planted last time may only be swollen or show a tiny root. Do not promise a sprout; that takes several days. Safety: keep bags sealed in case of mold, never taste seeds, check for legume allergies, and wash hands after handling.

segments.title: Name three needs
segments.description:
Each student writes or draws three things living things need on a sticky note.
Students stick their note under the picture of a living thing on the chart.
This is a quick check and is not graded.
segments.teacherNotes: Look for food, water and air. If a student writes sunlight for plants, accept it. Pull aside students who list toys or games and revisit the chart with them.

segments.title: Living or nonliving?
segments.description:
Hold up two cards from the sort and have students say living or nonliving together.
Remind students that next time we look more closely at how a bean seed changes.
segments.teacherNotes: Leave the chart on the wall. Students will use it again later in the unit.

keyIdeas: Living things grow and change, and they need things to survive. Nonliving things do not grow or need anything.
All living things need food, water and air. Plants make their own food using sunlight and water.
We can sort things into living and nonliving by asking what the thing does and needs.
The bean seed we planted is a living thing. It gets water from the damp paper towel and air from inside the bag. It uses food stored inside the seed to begin growing.

study.overview: Today you learned how to tell if something is alive. A cat, a sunflower and a bean seed are living things. A rock, a toy truck and a plastic ball are nonliving things. You also learned that living things need food, water and air to survive. To survive means to stay alive.

points.heading: Living things grow and change, and they need things
points.explanation: Living things are born, grow, reproduce and die. Along the way they need things to stay alive. Nonliving things do not grow and do not need anything. A cat is living. It grows from a kitten, and it needs food, water and air. A rock is nonliving. It does not eat, drink or breathe.

points.heading: Ask what it does and what it needs
points.explanation: To sort something into living or nonliving, ask what the thing does and needs. Does it grow? Does it need food, water and air? A sunflower is living, so it goes in the living group. A toy truck can move, but it does not grow or need food, so it stays in the nonliving group. Moving is not the only clue. A plant does not move much, but it is still alive.

points.heading: All living things need food, water and air
points.explanation: Animals like cats need food, water and air. Plants need water, air and sunlight. A plant makes its own food using sunlight and water. A plant does not eat soil. A sunflower is an example. It makes its own food from sunlight, water and air.

points.heading: The bean seed is a living thing
points.explanation: The bean seed we planted looks still, but it is alive because it will grow into a plant. It gets water from the damp paper towel. It gets air from inside the bag. It uses food stored inside the seed to begin growing. This is why we keep the bags sealed and look at them without opening them. Use your journal to draw any changes you see, like a bigger bean or a tiny root.

l_2d7b182b5f8b.title: From seed to sprout
l_2d7b182b5f8b.summary: Students look closely at soaked and sprouting beans and record the first changes in their journals.

segments.title: Dry bean, soaked bean
segments.description:
Hold up a dry bean seed and a soaked bean seed side by side.
Ask, “What is different?” Take three or four answers.
Say, “Today we look even closer, because the beans in our bags are changing.”
segments.teacherNotes: Expect: bigger, softer, wrinkly, smoother. Safety: students never put beans in their mouths. Use pinto or lima beans. Raw dry beans of any kind, including lima and kidney beans, are harmful to eat. Check for legume allergies before handling.

segments.title: Look inside the seed
segments.description:
Split a soaked bean in half under the document camera. Point out the seed coat, the stored food and the tiny baby plant.
Pass out hand lenses and show how to hold one close to the eye and move the bean toward it.
Show a prepared sprouting bean and point to the root, which came out first, and the small shoot that grows up.
segments.teacherNotes: Prepare ahead: soak extra beans overnight and split one. About a week before the unit starts, soak and bag extra beans, one per pair plus a few spares, so a root and a small shoot are visible by today. Do not split seeds in the classroom bags.

segments.title: Draw a seed and its root
segments.description:
Give each pair a tray with one prepared sprouting bean and two hand lenses. Each student draws the bean and its first root in the journal.
Students label the seed coat and the root, and write today’s date.
Walk around and ask, “Where does the root start? Which way does it point?”
segments.teacherNotes: Draw in pencil, large, filling half the page. Common mistake: drawing the root as a leaf or leaving the seed out. Model a first label for students who need it. Wash hands afterward.

segments.title: Check our own bags
segments.description:
Each student takes their sealed bag from the window and looks closely through the plastic with a hand lens.
Students record what they see in the journal: a drawing and one sentence, such as “The bean has a root” or “The seed has not changed yet.”
Students compare their bag to the prepared sprouting bean.
segments.teacherNotes: Bags stay sealed. Some beans may show only a tiny root or none; that is normal, and every seed grows at its own speed. If students see mold or a bad smell, they do not open the bag and tell you.

segments.title: How has it changed?
segments.description:
Gather on the rug. Students share with a partner, then the class, how their bean has changed since we planted it.
Use the sentence frame “At first the seed was ___. Now it ___.”
Return to the class chart “Living things need.” Ask, “What did the bean get from the damp towel and the bag?”
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: water from the towel, air from the bag, food stored in the seed. Accept “the seed got bigger” and “a root came out.” Gently correct “the seed is dead” for beans with no change yet: it may still be waking up.

segments.title: One change I can name
segments.description:
Each student tells a partner one change they saw in a bean today.
Then students show thumbs up if their journal page has a drawing, a label and a date.
This check-in is practice and is not graded.
segments.teacherNotes: Listen for the words root, sprout and seed coat. Note students who cannot find the root on their drawing and revisit it with them next time. Nothing is scored.

segments.title: Back to the window
segments.description:
Students check that their bags are still sealed and return them to the window.
Students wash their hands.
Say, “We will check our bean bags again next time. Think about what the sprout may do.”
segments.teacherNotes: Make sure bags are zipped and the paper towels are still damp. Add a few drops of water if a towel looks dry.

keyIdeas: A bean seed is covered by a seed coat that protects the baby plant and the stored food inside.
The seed swells as it takes in water. The root is the first plant part to come out. It grows out of the seed and down.
After the root, a shoot pushes up. It will grow into the stem and leaves. A seed with a root and a shoot is called a sprout.
Scientists observe closely, draw what they see and write the date, so they can tell how things change.

vocabulary.definition: The hard skin that covers a seed and protects the baby plant inside.

A tool that makes small things look bigger so we can observe them closely.

study.overview: Today you looked closely at beans that are waking up. You used a hand lens, drew a bean seed and its first root, and checked your own bean bag. Scientists look closely, draw what they see and write the date. That is how they can tell how things change.

points.heading: The seed coat protects the baby plant
points.explanation: A bean seed is covered by a seed coat. The seed coat protects the tiny baby plant and the stored food inside. When we split a soaked bean, we could see the seed coat, the stored food and the baby plant. Example: the dry bean was hard and small. The soaked bean was bigger and softer, but its seed coat still covered everything inside.

points.heading: The root comes out first, then the shoot
points.explanation: The seed swells as it takes in water. The root is the first plant part to come out. It grows out of the seed and down. After the root, a shoot pushes up. The shoot will grow into the stem and leaves. A seed with a root and a shoot is called a sprout. Example: on the prepared sprouting bean, the root had come out first and a small shoot was starting. In your drawing, the root points down and is not a leaf. Remember to draw the seed too.

points.heading: Seeds get what they need and grow at their own speed
points.explanation: The bean in your bag got water from the damp towel and air from the bag. It also had food stored inside the seed. Every seed grows at its own speed. Some beans show a tiny root and some show none yet. That is normal. A bean with no change may still be waking up. Example: you might write, “The seed has not changed yet.” Another student might write, “The bean has a root.” Both are good observations.

points.heading: Scientists draw, label and write the date
points.explanation: Good observing has three parts: a drawing, labels and a date. Draw the bean large, label the seed coat and the root, and write today’s date. Then you can compare your pages later. Example: you can use the sentence frame “At first the seed was ___. Now it ___.” to tell how your bean has changed, such as “At first the seed was small and hard. Now it is bigger and a root came out.” Next time, we will check our bean bags again. Think about what the sprout may do.

l_005e4970837e.title: Stages of a bean plant life cycle
l_005e4970837e.summary: Students name the stages from seed to adult plant and sequence picture cards of the bean life cycle.

segments.title: What changed in our bags?
segments.description:
Students take their sealed bags from the window and look closely, using a hand lens if they want.
They tell a partner one thing that is different since last time.
Call on two pairs to share. Ask which part came out first.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: the root came out first, then a small shoot. Bags stay sealed, since damp towels can grow mold. Students wash hands after handling. Bags go back to the window at the end of the lesson.

segments.title: Meet the five stages
segments.description:
Show five large picture cards one at a time on the board, or on the document camera: seed, sprout, seedling, adult plant, new seeds in a pod.
Name each stage and say what happens. A sprout becomes a seedling with its first green leaves. The adult plant grows flowers, and the flowers make pods.
Point out that the pod holds new seeds. Say that the new seeds can start the cycle again.
Students repeat each stage name and make a hand motion for it, such as a fist for the seed and arms rising for the seedling.
segments.teacherNotes: A bean plant takes about 8 weeks to flower and make pods, so use photos unless you planted pots about two months before the unit. Our beans will still be seeds or sprouts with a root and a small shoot. Use the photos to show stages we cannot observe yet. Common mistake: thinking the flower is the seed. Never let students eat raw beans or seeds. Check allergies.

segments.title: Put the bean cards in order
segments.description:
Give each pair one set of five bean life cycle cards, mixed up.
Pairs put the cards in order from seed to seed and say each stage name aloud as they place it.
When a pair finishes, they check against the board and fix any card that is out of place.
This is practice only and is not graded.
segments.teacherNotes:
Card set, in correct order:
1. Seed: a dry bean seed
2. Sprout: root and shoot coming out of the seed
3. Seedling: small plant with first green leaves
4. Adult plant: tall plant with flowers
5. New seeds: pod with beans inside
Common mistake: swapping seedling and adult plant. Prompt with ‘Which one is bigger?’. Make the sets ahead from photos or simple drawings, plus one large set for the board, and laminate them.

segments.title: Why is it a cycle?
segments.description:
Bring students to the rug with their card sets in the correct order.
Ask what comes after the new seeds in the pod. Ask what the old plant does when it is finished.
Students tell a partner which stage shows the plant reproducing. Then share with the class.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: the new seeds can be planted and grow into new plants. The pod stage shows reproducing. The old plant dries up and dies, as every living thing does eventually. Link back to the cat and chicken from before: born, grow, reproduce, die.

segments.title: Journal: our bean today
segments.description:
Students open their observation journals and write today’s date.
Each student draws their own bean as it looks now and labels the root and the shoot, if there is one.
Then they draw one arrow to a small box and sketch what stage they think comes next.
Students return their bags to the window.
segments.teacherNotes: Journal work is practice and is not graded. It builds the drawing-and-labeling skill used in the graded final assessment of one life cycle. Expected: a drawing that matches the student’s bean today. The predicted stage follows what they observe: seed to sprout, or sprout to seedling. Help with spelling of labels.

segments.title: Name that stage
segments.description:
Hold up the cards one at a time in mixed order.
Students say the stage name together, then show with fingers where it comes in the cycle, from one to five.
Note which stages the class still mixes up.
segments.teacherNotes: Not graded. Expected fingers: seed 1, sprout 2, seedling 3, adult plant 4, new seeds in pod 5. If many students miss seedling and adult plant, revisit the leaves and flowers on the cards. Note which students need help before the final assessment.

segments.title: Seed to seed
segments.description:
Students say the five stages in order with their hand motions.
Remind them that the new seeds start the cycle again.
segments.teacherNotes: Finish with the sentence frame: A bean plant starts as a seed and ends with new seeds. Keep the five cards on display for later in the unit, when we compare life cycles.

keyIdeas: A bean plant’s life cycle has stages in a fixed order: seed, sprout, seedling, adult plant, and new seeds in pods.
A sprout grows into a seedling with its first green leaves. The seedling grows into an adult plant with flowers.
Flowers on the adult plant make pods. The pods hold new bean seeds, so the plant reproduces.
The new seeds can be planted, and the life cycle starts again. That is why we order the cards from seed to seed.

study.overview: A bean plant has a life cycle. That means it goes through the same stages in the same order, and then the cycle starts again. There are five stages: seed, sprout, seedling, adult plant, and new seeds in a pod. We put the cards in order from seed to seed because the new seeds can start the cycle again.

points.heading: The five stages in order
points.explanation: The stages always come in this order: 1. seed, 2. sprout, 3. seedling, 4. adult plant, 5. new seeds in a pod. A seed is a dry bean. A sprout has a root and a shoot coming out of the seed. A seedling is a small plant with its first green leaves. An adult plant is tall and has flowers. Then the pod has new beans inside. Try saying them with your hand motions: a fist for the seed, and arms rising for the seedling.

points.heading: How a sprout becomes an adult plant
points.explanation: A sprout grows into a seedling when it gets its first green leaves. Then the seedling grows into an adult plant with flowers. If two cards look alike, ask yourself, “Which one is bigger?” The adult plant is bigger than the seedling, so it comes later. Our beans in the bags may still be seeds, or they may be sprouts. Photos help us see the stages we cannot watch yet.

points.heading: Why it is a cycle
points.explanation: The flowers on the adult plant make pods. The pods hold new bean seeds, so the plant reproduces. The flower is not the seed. The seeds are inside the pod. Those new seeds can be planted, and then they grow into new bean plants. The old plant dries up and dies, as every living thing does in the end. Living things are born, grow, reproduce and die. You can say it like this: A bean plant starts as a seed and ends with new seeds.

points.heading: Drawing your bean in the journal
points.explanation: In your observation journal, draw your own bean the way it looks today and label the root and the shoot. Then draw an arrow to a small box and sketch the stage you think comes next. For example, if your bean is a sprout, you might draw a seedling with green leaves. This is practice for drawing and labeling a life cycle later in the unit.

l_4a3e15ece1b9.title: Butterfly life cycle: egg to caterpillar
l_4a3e15ece1b9.summary: Students hear a picture book about a butterfly and learn the egg and larva stages.

segments.title: Bean bags and a butterfly question
segments.description:
Students take their sealed bean bags from the window and look closely with a hand lens.
Each student adds the date and one new drawing or word to the journal page for their bean.
Then ask, “We have watched a plant change. What do you think a butterfly looks like when it is just starting its life?”
Take two or three quick guesses and put the bags back.
segments.teacherNotes: Bags stay sealed. Do not open them. Students wash hands if a bag leaks. Expect guesses like “a small butterfly.” Do not correct yet. Come back to the guesses in the close.

segments.title: Read aloud: a butterfly picture book
segments.description:
Gather students on the rug and read aloud The Very Hungry Caterpillar by Eric Carle.
Before reading, say, “This is a made-up story. Some parts are true and some are pretend. Listen for how the story begins and what the little animal does all day.”
Pause after the first page and after the caterpillar gets big. Ask, “What stage is this?”
Tell students that in real life a caterpillar eats leaves, not cake or pie. Explain that the butterfly stage the book calls a cocoon is called a chrysalis.
segments.teacherNotes: Read the book aloud. Use your own words when explaining its science. Expected answers: the story begins with a tiny egg on a leaf; the animal eats and eats and gets bigger. Misconception: the book shows junk food. Real caterpillars eat leaves. The book skips molting, so mention it next. Molting is not a stage. Check allergy notes: no food is handled.

segments.title: Egg and caterpillar: what we see
segments.description:
Show large photo cards of a monarch egg on a milkweed leaf, a newly hatched monarch caterpillar, and a big caterpillar.
Name each stage: egg, then larva, also called a caterpillar. Add the cards to the board in order.
Point out that the egg is tiny, about the size of a pinhead, and that the caterpillar hatches and eats leaves.
Show a photo of a caterpillar next to its shed skin and say that it molts to get bigger.
segments.teacherNotes: Students add egg, larva, caterpillar and molt to the word wall. Link the order to the bean cards from last time: stages go in a fixed order. Fact: a monarch caterpillar molts four times as it grows. Use photos only. No live insects. If a real milkweed leaf is shown, students must not touch it, because the sap can irritate skin and eyes.

segments.title: How much does a caterpillar grow?
segments.description:
Give each pair three prepared paper strips and a mat. Each strip shows a caterpillar length.
Pairs lay the strips side by side and decide which one is longer.
Then they put the strips in order from shortest to longest and tape them to the mat.
Share one pair’s mat and ask, “What do you notice about how the caterpillar changes?”
segments.teacherNotes:
Strips are prepared in advance, rough sizes, no measuring. Items:
1. Newly hatched caterpillar, a very short stub. Shortest.
2. Halfway grown caterpillar, about 1 inch. Middle.
3. Full-grown caterpillar, about 2 inches. Longest.
Expected: the full-grown strip is longer than the others. Students say it grows a lot. Do not ask for numbers or fractions. Use scissors only to prepare strips, not in class.

segments.title: Why does a caterpillar eat so much?
segments.description:
Ask, “Why do you think the caterpillar eats leaves all day?”
Students turn and talk to a partner, then share with the class.
Connect to the bean seed, which used stored food to start growing. The caterpillar gets its food by eating leaves.
Sum up together: it eats so it can grow bigger and get ready for the next stage.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected answer: food gives it energy and helps it grow. Misconception: the caterpillar is hungry because it is lazy, or it only eats for fun. Another: the caterpillar is already a butterfly. Redirect: it is still the larva stage. Prompt shy students with a sentence frame: “The caterpillar eats so it can ___.”

segments.title: Journal: egg and caterpillar
segments.description:
Students open their observation journals to a new page.
They draw a leaf with a tiny egg and a caterpillar next to it.
They label the drawing with the words egg and caterpillar. They add the date.
Early finishers add a sentence that says why the caterpillar eats.
segments.teacherNotes: This is practice, not graded. It prepares students for the final drawing-and-labeling assessment of one life cycle, which is the only graded work. Show a label with an arrow as a model. Expected: a small egg on a leaf and a larger caterpillar. Spelling can be sounded out. Crayons and pencils only.

segments.title: Egg or caterpillar?
segments.description:
Each student gets an egg card and a caterpillar card.
Read each clue aloud. Students hold up the card that fits.
Go through all five clues quickly.
segments.teacherNotes:
Short check, not graded. Prepare one small egg card and one caterpillar card per student (a quick drawing is fine). Clues and answers:
1. I am tiny and round and stuck to a leaf. Egg.
2. I eat leaves all day. Caterpillar.
3. I hatch out of an egg. Caterpillar.
4. I cannot move or eat. Egg.
5. I shed my skin so I can get bigger. Caterpillar.
Note who hesitates on clue 3 and revisit later in the unit.

segments.title: Back to our guesses
segments.description:
Return to the opening question about how a butterfly starts its life.
Students say, “A butterfly starts as an ___ and then becomes a ___.”
Tell them that next time they will see what the caterpillar does when it is done growing.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: egg, then caterpillar. Bean bags stay in the window. Students wash hands before leaving if they touched bags.

keyIdeas: A butterfly’s life cycle starts with an egg. A monarch butterfly lays a tiny egg on a leaf.
A caterpillar hatches from the egg. The caterpillar is the larva stage of a butterfly.
A caterpillar’s main job is to eat and grow. It eats leaves almost all the time.
A caterpillar’s skin does not stretch, so it sheds its skin, or molts, to get bigger.
The egg and the caterpillar come first in the butterfly’s life cycle, and the other stages follow in the same fixed order.

study.overview: Today you learned how a butterfly’s life begins. A butterfly starts as an egg. A caterpillar hatches from the egg. The caterpillar spends its time eating leaves and growing. You also drew an egg and a caterpillar in your observation journal.

points.heading: The egg is the first stage
points.explanation: A butterfly’s life cycle starts with an egg. A monarch butterfly lays a tiny egg on a leaf. The egg is about the size of a pinhead. It does not move or eat. In the photo cards, the egg was a tiny round dot on a milkweed leaf. When you finish the sentence “A butterfly starts as an ___,” the answer is egg. A butterfly does not start out as a small butterfly.

points.heading: The caterpillar is the larva stage
points.explanation: A caterpillar hatches from the egg. The caterpillar is the larva stage of a butterfly. It is still not a butterfly. Think of the clue “I hatch out of an egg.” The answer is caterpillar. The egg and the caterpillar come first, and the other stages follow in the same fixed order, just like the stages of your bean plant.

points.heading: A caterpillar eats and grows
points.explanation: A caterpillar’s main job is to eat and grow. It eats leaves almost all the time. In the story The Very Hungry Caterpillar, the caterpillar eats cake and pie, but a real caterpillar eats leaves. Food gives it energy and helps it grow. Remember the paper strips: a newly hatched caterpillar is a very short stub, a halfway grown one is about 1 inch, and a full-grown one is about 2 inches. The caterpillar eats so it can grow bigger and get ready for the next stage.

points.heading: A caterpillar molts to get bigger
points.explanation: A caterpillar’s skin does not stretch. When it gets too big for its skin, it sheds the skin. This is called molting. In the photo, you saw a caterpillar next to its shed skin. A monarch caterpillar molts four times as it grows. The story did not tell about molting, but it is part of how a real caterpillar gets bigger.

l_2fb84d4d6ec5.title: Butterfly life cycle: chrysalis to butterfly
l_2fb84d4d6ec5.summary: Students learn the pupa and adult stages and put all four butterfly stages in order with picture cards.

segments.title: Bean check and a question
segments.description:
Students take their sealed bean bags from the window and look closely, with a hand lens if they want.
Each student tells a partner one thing that looks different since last time. Students write today’s date in their bean observation journals and draw what they see.
Then ask, “Last time our caterpillar ate and ate. What do you think it does when it is all done growing?”
Take two or three guesses and say, “Today we find out.”
segments.teacherNotes: Bags stay sealed. Students wash hands after handling them. Beans are never tasted. Likely changes: a longer root, a bigger sprout, a split seed coat. Guesses about the caterpillar may include “it sleeps” or “it turns into a butterfly.” Welcome both guesses, then explain that it is not sleeping: it becomes a pupa, and its body changes.

segments.title: Meet the chrysalis
segments.description:
Show a large photo of a full-grown monarch caterpillar hanging upside down from a twig in a J shape.
Say, “It sheds its skin one last time. A hard case forms around it. The case is called a chrysalis, and this stage is the pupa.”

Students answer with a thumbs up or down, and then say “chrysalis” and “pupa” together.

points.heading: The chrysalis is the case, and pupa is the stage
points.explanation: When a caterpillar is done growing, it hangs from a twig or leaf. It sheds its skin one last time. Then a hard case forms around it. The case is called a chrysalis. The stage of life inside it is called the pupa stage. In our photo, a green chrysalis with gold dots hung still. A chrysalis does not eat and it does not move around. It only wiggles if it is touched.

points.heading: A lot happens inside the chrysalis
points.explanation: The chrysalis looks still and quiet, but the inside is busy. The caterpillar’s body changes into a butterfly’s body. It does not just get bigger. It changes into something new. This change is called metamorphosis. A butterfly’s body has wings, legs, antennae and a long mouth for sipping. Remember the three photos: first a green chrysalis, then a chrysalis turning clear with orange and black wings showing through, then a butterfly coming out.

points.heading: A new butterfly comes out
points.explanation: After about ten days to two weeks, a monarch butterfly comes out of the chrysalis. This is the adult stage. Its wings are wet and crumpled at first. The butterfly waits for them to dry before it flies. That takes a few hours. Later it sips nectar from flowers for food.

points.heading: Four stages in a fixed order make a cycle
points.explanation: The butterfly life cycle always goes in this order: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. The caterpillar must finish eating and growing before it becomes a chrysalis, so the chrysalis comes before the butterfly. Then the adult butterfly lays eggs on a leaf. A new caterpillar hatches from a new egg, and the cycle starts again. The butterfly does not turn back into the old caterpillar. This is like a bean plant, where new seeds can grow into new plants.

l_e5528d3a28fe.summary: Students learn how frog eggs in water hatch into tadpoles that swim and breathe with gills.

segments.title: Bean bags and a frog question
segments.description:
Each student takes a sealed bean bag from the window and looks closely at what has changed, using a hand lens if they want.
Students tell a partner one change they see. In their observation journals, students write today’s date and draw what their bean looks like today.
Then ask, “A butterfly starts as an egg on a leaf. Where do you think a frog starts its life?”
Take a few guesses and say that we will find out today.
segments.teacherNotes: Bags stay sealed and are never opened. Students wash hands after handling them. Guesses may include land, trees or the pond. Accept all guesses and revisit them at the end of the lesson. Keep this quick so the rest of the time is protected.

segments.title: Frog eggs in the pond
segments.description:
Show a large photo of frogspawn: a clump of clear jelly with a dark dot in each egg, floating in a pond.
Say, “Frogs lay their eggs in water. The eggs are soft and covered in jelly.”
Students point out the dark dots, the jelly and the water in the photo.
Compare with last time: a butterfly egg is tiny and sits on a leaf, but a frog egg sits in water.
segments.teacherNotes: Use a photo only. Do not collect wild frogspawn: it is illegal in some places and harms ponds. Each dark dot is a tiny baby frog starting to grow. Common mistake: thinking frog eggs have a hard shell like a bird egg. They are soft and jelly-covered. Some tree frogs lay eggs on leaves, but we use pond frogs.

segments.title: Meet the tadpole
segments.description:
Show a photo of a newly hatched tadpole with feathery gills clearly visible on the sides of its head, next to a simple labeled diagram showing head, tail and gills.
Say, “The egg hatches and a tadpole comes out. It has a tail, no legs, and it lives in water.”
Students trace the tail and the gills in the air with a finger.
Explain, “A tadpole swims by wiggling its tail, and it breathes underwater with gills.”
Leave the photo and diagram displayed for the journal drawing.
segments.teacherNotes: Choose a newly hatched tadpole photo where the external gills show clearly. Gills are hidden under the skin on bigger tadpoles, so do not use a photo of a large swimming tadpole. Common mistake: thinking tadpoles are fish. Say they become frogs. Say a tadpole’s gills work like our nose and lungs do for air.

segments.title: What can a tadpole do?
segments.description:
Give each pair four statement cards and a two-column mat labeled “Tadpole can” and “Tadpole cannot yet”.
Pairs read each card aloud, decide together and place it on the mat.
Bring the class back and read each card with the class answering together.
This is practice and is not graded.
segments.teacherNotes:
Cards, with answers:
Swims by wiggling its tail: Tadpole can
Breathes underwater with gills: Tadpole can
Lives in the pond: Tadpole can
Hops on land with legs: Tadpole cannot yet
Print pictures beside the words for early readers. Read cards aloud to pairs who need it.

segments.title: Journal: egg and tadpole
segments.description:
Students open their observation journals to a new page and write today’s date.
Using the displayed photo and diagram, each student draws one frog egg clump with jelly and dark dots, and one newly hatched tadpole with its tail and gills.
Students label tail and gills, copying the words from the board.
Students who finish early add water around their drawings.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep the photo and labeled diagram visible the whole time. Expect simple drawings: an oval with a dot, and a tadpole with a tail and a feathery shape for gills. Praise the details students see. Not graded. Eggs, then tadpole, are drawn in order across the page. Use pencils or crayons only.

segments.title: Finish the sentence
segments.description:
Students use mini whiteboards to finish two sentences.
Say, “Frogs lay their eggs in ___.”
Then say, “A tadpole breathes with ___.”
Students hold up boards for a quick check.
segments.teacherNotes:
Sentences and expected answers:
Frogs lay their eggs in ___: water (a pond)
A tadpole breathes with ___: gills
Drawings are accepted from students who cannot spell yet. Not graded. Note who is unsure and revisit them during journals next time.

segments.title: Back to our guesses
segments.description:
Return to the opening question about where a frog starts its life.
Students tell a partner the answer with the words egg, water and tadpole.
Say, “Next time we see how the tadpole changes and grows legs.”
Students return bean bags to the window and check they are sealed.
segments.teacherNotes: Share a correct answer such as “A frog starts as an egg in water, then hatches into a tadpole.” Students wash hands after handling the bags.

keyIdeas: A frog’s life cycle starts with an egg. Frogs lay their eggs in water, such as a pond, in a clump of clear jelly called frogspawn.
A tadpole hatches from the egg. It looks very different from a grown frog: it has a tail and no legs.
A tadpole lives in water all the time. It swims by wiggling its tail and breathes underwater with gills.
Tadpoles spend their time eating and growing. The egg and the tadpole come first in the frog’s life cycle, and the other stages follow in a fixed order.

study.overview: Today you learned how a frog’s life begins. A frog starts as an egg in water. The egg hatches into a tadpole. A tadpole looks very different from a grown frog, and it lives in the water all the time. Eggs come first in the life cycle, and tadpoles come next. This guide will help you remember what you saw in the photos and drew in your journal.

points.heading: Frogs lay eggs in water
points.explanation: A frog’s life cycle starts with an egg. Frogs lay their eggs in water, such as a pond. The eggs come in a clump of clear jelly called frogspawn. In the photo, each egg had a dark dot inside it. The eggs are soft and covered in jelly. Each dark dot is a tiny baby frog starting to grow. A butterfly egg is tiny and sits on a leaf, but a frog egg sits in water. Try this: say, “A frog starts as an egg in water.”

points.heading: A tadpole hatches from the egg
points.explanation: The egg hatches and a tadpole comes out. A tadpole does not look like a grown frog. It has a tail and no legs. A tadpole is not a fish. It is a baby frog that will change and become a frog. In the photo of a newly hatched tadpole, you could see feathery gills on the sides of its head. In your journal, you drew a tadpole with a tail and gills and labeled them.

points.heading: A tadpole lives and breathes in water
points.explanation: A tadpole lives in water all the time. It swims by wiggling its tail. It breathes underwater with gills. A tadpole’s gills work like our nose and lungs do for air. Think about the card sort: “Swims by wiggling its tail,” “Breathes underwater with gills” and “Lives in the pond” went under “Tadpole can.” “Hops on land with legs” went under “Tadpole cannot yet.” Tadpoles spend their time eating and growing.

points.heading: The stages come in order
points.explanation: The egg and the tadpole come first in the frog’s life cycle. The other stages follow in a fixed order. In your journal, you drew the egg clump first and the tadpole next, across the page. Next time we see how the tadpole changes and grows legs. Check yourself: finish the sentences “Frogs lay their eggs in ___” (water, or a pond) and “A tadpole breathes with ___” (gills).

l_90a5a4ad604a.summary: Students see how tadpoles grow legs, lose tails and become adult frogs, then sequence the frog stages.

segments.title: Bean check and a tadpole question
segments.description:
Students take their sealed bean bags from the window and look closely with a hand lens. Each student tells a partner one change in the bean since last time.
Show the tadpole photo from last time and ask, “A tadpole has a tail and gills. Do you think it stays like this forever?”
Take three guesses and say, “Let’s find out how a tadpole changes.”
segments.teacherNotes: Bags stay sealed. Never open them: mold can grow in damp bags. Students wash hands after handling. Likely guesses: it turns into a frog, it grows legs. Accept all and say the photos will show.

segments.title: From tadpole to froglet
segments.description:
Show four large photos one at a time: a tadpole with a long tail, a tadpole with back legs, a tadpole with four legs and a shorter tail, and a froglet.
Point to the back legs and say, “The hind legs grow first. Then the front legs grow.”
Say, “The tail gets shorter. The gills go away and lungs grow inside. A froglet breathes air with its lungs.”
Students kick their legs for hind legs, reach out their arms for front legs, and make a tail shrinking with one finger.
segments.teacherNotes: Use photos only; do not handle live tadpoles. Misconception: the tail falls off. It shrinks as the body uses it. Lungs are inside, so students cannot see them. Time varies: weeks to months, depending on the kind of frog.

segments.title: The adult frog and the cycle
segments.description:
Show a photo of an adult frog sitting at the edge of a pond. Say, “This is the adult frog stage. It has no tail and it breathes with lungs. It can live on land and in water.”
Say, “An adult frog eats insects.”
Show the frogspawn photo from last time and ask, “Where do new eggs come from?”
Say, “The adult frog lays new eggs, so the cycle starts again.”
segments.teacherNotes: Expected answer: from the adult frog. Connect to the butterfly and bean cycles: each one is a circle that starts again. A froglet is not yet an adult, so it does not lay eggs.

segments.title: Put the frog cards in order
segments.description:
Give each pair one set of four mixed-up picture cards: egg, tadpole, froglet, adult frog.
Partners put the cards in order from egg to adult frog and tell each other what changes between two cards.
Walk around and ask, “How do you know the froglet comes before the adult frog?”
Then gather on the rug and check the order together by pointing to each card on the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Ungraded practice. Expected order: egg, tadpole, froglet, adult frog. Common mistake: swapping tadpole and froglet. Prompt: which one still has gills? Early finishers add an arrow from adult frog back to egg.

segments.title: Journal: froglet and adult frog
segments.description:
Students open their journals to the egg and tadpole page from last time and write today’s date.
They draw a froglet and an adult frog next to the tadpole.
They label legs, tail and froglet, and write “adult frog” under the last drawing.
segments.teacherNotes: Ungraded practice for the final drawing and labeling task. Show the cards as models. Ask each student, “What changed from the tadpole?” Expected: legs, shorter or no tail. Allow short labels; spelling need not be perfect.

segments.title: Which stage am I?
segments.description:
Read each clue aloud. Pairs hold up the matching card from their set.
Repeat any clue that splits the class.
This is a quick check-in and is not graded.
segments.teacherNotes:
Clues and answers:
1. I am a clump of clear jelly with black dots. Egg.
2. I have a long tail and gills and live only in water. Tadpole.
3. I have four legs, a short tail and lungs, and I am small. Froglet.
4. I have no tail and I breathe with lungs. Adult frog.
5. I lay the new eggs. Adult frog.

segments.title: Say the stages and back to the window
segments.description:
Students say the four frog stages in order with hand motions: a fist for the egg, a wiggling finger for the tadpole, a small hop for the froglet, a big hop for the adult frog.
Each student tells a partner one way a tadpole changes.
Students check that their bean bags are still sealed and return them to the window.
Say, “Next time we compare the bean, the butterfly and the frog.”
segments.teacherNotes: Listen for legs, tail getting shorter, lungs or breathing air. If a student mentions the class chart, point to “air” and say an adult frog gets air with lungs.

keyIdeas: A tadpole grows back legs first, then front legs. Its tail gets shorter and shorter as it grows.
A tadpole breathes with gills. As it changes, it grows lungs and loses its gills, so a froglet can breathe air.
A froglet is a young frog with four legs and a short bit of tail left. It grows into an adult frog with no tail.
The frog life cycle has four stages in a fixed order: egg, tadpole, froglet, adult frog. The adult frog lays new eggs, so the cycle starts again.

vocabulary.definition: A young frog that has four legs and a short bit of tail left.
Body parts inside that let an animal breathe air. A tadpole has gills, and a frog has lungs.
The back legs. A tadpole grows these first.

slides.title: Frog life cycle: froglet to adult frog
bullets: How does a tadpole change?
Put the frog stages in order
slides.notes: Begin with the bean check. Students take their sealed bean bags from the window and look closely with a hand lens. Each student tells a partner one change in the bean since last time. Bags stay sealed. Never open them, because mold can grow in damp bags. Students wash hands after handling. Then show the tadpole photo from last time and ask, ‘A tadpole has a tail and gills. Do you think it stays like this forever?’ Take three guesses. Likely guesses: it turns into a frog, it grows legs. Accept all and say, ‘Let’s find out how a tadpole changes.’

slides.title: Does a tadpole stay like this forever?
bullets: A tadpole has a tail and gills
What do you think will happen?
slides.notes: Keep the tadpole photo from last time on screen. Take three guesses and accept all of them. Say the photos will show us. This question sets the purpose for the next part of the lesson.

slides.title: From tadpole to froglet
bullets: Hind legs grow first
Then the front legs grow
The tail gets shorter and shorter
Gills go away and lungs grow inside
A froglet breathes air with its lungs
slides.notes: Show four large photos one at a time: a tadpole with a long tail, a tadpole with back legs, a tadpole with four legs and a shorter tail, and a froglet. Point to the back legs and say, ‘The hind legs grow first. Then the front legs grow.’ Then say, ‘The tail gets shorter. The gills go away and lungs grow inside. A froglet breathes air with its lungs.’ Students kick their legs for hind legs, reach out their arms for front legs, and make a tail shrinking with one finger. Use photos only. Do not handle live tadpoles. The tail does not fall off. It shrinks as the body uses it. Lungs are inside, so students cannot see them. Time varies from weeks to months, depending on the kind of frog.

slides.title: The adult frog and the cycle
bullets: A froglet has four legs and a short bit of tail
An adult frog has no tail
It breathes with lungs
It lives on land and in water
It lays new eggs
slides.notes: Show a photo of an adult frog sitting at the edge of a pond. Say, ‘This is the adult frog stage. It has no tail and it breathes with lungs. It can live on land and in water.’ Say, ‘An adult frog eats insects.’ Show the frogspawn photo from last time and ask, ‘Where do new eggs come from?’ Expected answer: from the adult frog. Say, ‘The adult frog lays new eggs, so the cycle starts again.’ Connect to the butterfly and bean cycles: each one is a circle that starts again. A froglet is not yet an adult, so it does not lay eggs.

slides.title: Put the frog cards in order
bullets: Work with your partner
Order the cards from egg to adult frog
Tell what changes between two cards
Check the order on the board
slides.notes: Give each pair one set of four mixed-up picture cards: egg, tadpole, froglet, adult frog. This is ungraded practice. Walk around and ask, ‘How do you know the froglet comes before the adult frog?’ Common mistake: swapping tadpole and froglet. Prompt: which one still has gills? Then gather on the rug and check the order together by pointing to each card on the board. Expected order: egg, tadpole, froglet, adult frog. Early finishers add an arrow from adult frog back to egg.

slides.title: Journal: froglet and adult frog
bullets: Open to the egg and tadpole page
Write today’s date
Draw a froglet and an adult frog
Label legs, tail and froglet
Write adult frog under the last drawing
slides.notes: This is ungraded practice for the final drawing and labeling task. Show the cards as models. Ask each student, ‘What changed from the tadpole?’ Expected: legs, shorter or no tail. Allow short labels. Spelling need not be perfect.

slides.title: Which stage am I?
bullets: Listen to each clue
Hold up the matching card
slides.notes: This is a quick check-in and is not graded. Read each clue aloud. Repeat any clue that splits the class. Clues and answers: 1. I am a clump of clear jelly with black dots. Egg. 2. I have a long tail and gills and live only in water. Tadpole. 3. I have four legs, a short tail and lungs, and I am small. Froglet. 4. I have no tail and I breathe with lungs. Adult frog. 5. I lay the new eggs. Adult frog.

slides.title: Say the stages and back to the window
bullets: Egg: make a fist
Tadpole: wiggle a finger
Froglet: a small hop
Adult frog: a big hop
Tell a partner one way a tadpole changes
slides.notes: Students say the four frog stages in order with the hand motions. Each student tells a partner one way a tadpole changes. Listen for legs, tail getting shorter, lungs or breathing air. If a student mentions the class chart, point to ‘air’ and say an adult frog gets air with lungs. Students check that their bean bags are still sealed and return them to the window. Say, ‘Next time we compare the bean, the butterfly and the frog.’

study.overview: Today you learned how a tadpole changes into a froglet and then into an adult frog. You also put the four frog stages in order. The frog life cycle goes egg, tadpole, froglet, adult frog. Then the adult frog lays new eggs, so the cycle starts again.

points.heading: A tadpole grows legs and its tail gets shorter
points.explanation: A tadpole starts with a long tail and no legs. First the back legs grow. These are the hind legs. Then the front legs grow. As the tadpole gets bigger, its tail gets shorter and shorter. The tail does not fall off. It shrinks. For example, in the photos, the tadpole with four legs had a shorter tail than the tadpole with only back legs.

points.heading: Gills change to lungs
points.explanation: A tadpole breathes with gills and lives only in water. As it changes, lungs grow inside its body and the gills go away. Lungs are inside, so we cannot see them in a photo. A froglet breathes air with its lungs. For example, if someone asks which stage still has gills, the answer is the tadpole.

points.heading: A froglet is a young frog
points.explanation: A froglet has four legs and a short bit of tail left. It is small. It is not an adult yet. Later the froglet grows into an adult frog with no tail. An adult frog breathes with lungs and can live on land and in water. It eats insects. For example, if you see a small frog with four legs and a short tail, it is a froglet.

points.heading: The frog life cycle is a circle
points.explanation: The four stages always go in the same order: egg, tadpole, froglet, adult frog. Frog eggs come in a clump of clear jelly with black dots, called frogspawn. The adult frog lays new eggs, so the cycle starts again. The bean and the butterfly also have cycles that start again. To check your order, ask which card still has gills. That card is the tadpole, and it comes before the froglet.

l_6f3458b7fab6.title: Comparing three life cycles
l_6f3458b7fab6.summary: Students compare the bean, butterfly and frog cycles, share their journals and see that all living things are born, grow, reproduce and die.

segments.title: Bean bags and a big question
segments.description:
Students take their sealed bean bags from the window and look closely, using a hand lens if they want.
Each student tells a partner one change in the bean since last time.
Ask, “Is our bean doing something the butterfly and the frog also do?” Take two or three quick answers and say we will find out today.
segments.teacherNotes: Safety: bags stay sealed so mold spores are not released. Beans are never eaten, and some children have bean or legume allergies, so check your allergy list. Students wash hands after handling the bags. Expect answers like “a root came out” or “it has a green shoot.”

segments.title: Three cycles in a row
segments.description:
Post three rows of picture cards on the board: the five bean cards, the four butterfly cards and the four frog cards, each in order.
Students say each row’s stages aloud with hand motions: seed to seed, egg to butterfly, egg to adult frog.
Point to the first card in each row and ask, “Which cycles start with an egg? Which starts with a seed?”
Explain that to compare is to look for how things are alike and how they are different.
segments.teacherNotes: Use the same large cards from earlier. Frog motions: fist for the egg, wiggling finger for the tadpole, small hop for the froglet, big hop for the adult frog. Expected answer: butterfly and frog start with an egg, bean starts with a seed. Do not reteach the stages; this is a quick recall.

segments.title: Alike and different: butterfly and frog
segments.description:
Give each pair a two-circle mat labeled “Butterfly” and “Frog”, with the overlap labeled “Both”, and six small picture-and-word cards.
Pairs read each card and place it in one circle or in the overlap.
Walk around and ask, “How do you know it goes there?”
Pairs then finish one sentence frame: “A butterfly and a frog are alike because ___.”
This is practice and is not graded.
segments.teacherNotes:
Cards and answers:
Starts as an egg: Both
Makes a chrysalis: Butterfly
Has a tail and gills when young: Frog
Grows bigger as it gets older: Both
Has four stages in a fixed order: Both
Adult lays new eggs: Both
Common mistake: putting “tail” in Both because a froglet has a short tail. Point back to the tadpole card. Pair early finishers with a pair that needs help.

segments.title: What all living things share
segments.description:
Look at the “Both” circle. Say that the bean, the butterfly and the frog also do four things.
Write four words on the board, one at a time, with a hand motion for each: born, grow, reproduce, die.
Tie each word to an example: a caterpillar hatches from an egg, a caterpillar grows, an adult frog lays eggs, and a bean plant dries up after its pods hold seeds.
Say, “All living things are born, grow, reproduce and die.” Students repeat it with the motions.
segments.teacherNotes: Define reproduce as making new living things of the same kind. Keep the talk about death calm and matter-of-fact: it is a normal part of every life cycle. Some students may think of a pet or a family member, so allow quiet sharing. Do not give lifespans.

segments.title: Journal share: is our bean living?
segments.description:
Students open their observation journals to the newest bean page and share it with a partner.
Bring the class together and read the four words from the board.
Ask, “Which of the four has our bean done so far?” Students point to their journal drawings as proof.
Ask, “Which of these things have we not seen our bean do yet?”
segments.teacherNotes: Expected answers: for a plant, sprouting is like being born: the tiny plant inside the seed comes out, the way a caterpillar hatches from an egg. The seed was already living before it sprouted, just as an egg is. New roots and leaves in our drawings show growth. We have not seen it reproduce or die. It is still young and has not grown flowers or pods with new seeds. The bean plant in the cards does all four. Link to the class chart “Living things need”: living things need these things so they can keep growing.

segments.title: Finish the sentence
segments.description:
Students use mini whiteboards to finish two sentences.
They hold up their boards for you to scan.
Give a thumbs up for correct boards and re-ask the question for any that are unclear.
segments.teacherNotes:
Sentences and expected answers:
A butterfly and a frog are alike because both start as an egg (also accept grow, or lay eggs as adults).
All living things are born, grow, reproduce and die.
Use the boards to spot students who still need support before the drawing task next time. Not graded.

segments.title: Say it and look ahead
segments.description:
Students stand and say “born, grow, reproduce, die” with the hand motions.
Tell them that next time each student will draw one life cycle and label its stages.
Explain that the drawing is scored as Excellent, Good, Developing or Beginning, and that today’s work was practice.
Students return their bean bags to the window.
segments.teacherNotes: Tell students they may choose the bean, the butterfly or the frog next time. Keep a set of picture cards for each cycle ready for them. Check that bags are sealed before they go back to the window.

keyIdeas: The bean, the butterfly and the frog each have stages in a fixed order, and each cycle starts again. We can compare two cycles to see how they are alike and different.

The butterfly and the frog are alike: both start as an egg, both look very different when young, and both grow into adults that lay new eggs. They are different too: a butterfly makes a chrysalis, and a frog has a tadpole with a tail and gills.
All living things are born, grow, reproduce and die. The bean, the butterfly and the frog all do these four things.
To reproduce means to make new living things of the same kind. An adult bean plant makes seeds, an adult butterfly lays eggs, and an adult frog lays eggs.

vocabulary.definition: To look at two things and tell how they are alike and how they are different.
To make new living things of the same kind, like a plant making seeds or a frog laying eggs.

study.overview: Today you compared the bean, the butterfly and the frog. Each one has stages in a fixed order, and each cycle starts again. You found how two cycles are alike and different. You also learned four things that all living things share: they are born, grow, reproduce and die.

points.heading: Comparing two life cycles
points.explanation: To compare is to look for how things are alike and how they are different. Look at the butterfly and the frog. They are alike because both start as an egg, both look very different when young, and both grow into adults that lay new eggs. They are different too. A butterfly makes a chrysalis. A frog has a tadpole with a tail and gills when it is young. So “makes a chrysalis” goes in the Butterfly circle, and “has a tail and gills when young” goes in the Frog circle.

points.heading: What all living things share
points.explanation: All living things are born, grow, reproduce and die. The bean, the butterfly and the frog all do these four things. Here is an example for each word. A caterpillar hatches from an egg, so it is born. A caterpillar grows. An adult frog lays eggs, so it reproduces. A bean plant dries up after its pods hold seeds, which is part of dying. Death is a normal part of every life cycle.

points.heading: What reproduce means
points.explanation: To reproduce means to make new living things of the same kind. This is how each cycle starts again. An adult bean plant makes seeds. An adult butterfly lays eggs. An adult frog lays eggs. The new seeds and eggs grow into new plants and animals of the same kind.

points.heading: Is our bean living?
points.explanation: Look at your observation journal and ask which of the four things our bean has done so far. Our bean seed was already living before it sprouted. For a plant, sprouting is like being born: the tiny plant comes out of the seed, the way a caterpillar hatches from an egg. New roots and leaves in your drawings show that it grows. We have not seen our bean reproduce or die yet. It is still young and has not grown flowers or pods with new seeds. The bean plant in the picture cards does all four. Living things need the things on our class chart so they can keep growing.

l_670c582e6107.title: Draw and label a life cycle
l_670c582e6107.summary: Students choose one life cycle, draw and label its stages, and check their work against a simple rubric.

segments.title: Bean check and say the stages
segments.description:
Students take their sealed bean bags from the window and look closely, with a hand lens if they want.
Students open their journals to their first bean drawing and compare it with the bean in the bag. Each student tells a partner, “At first my bean was ___. Now it ___.”
Say, “Our beans sprouted and grew. After today they go into cups of soil, so we can watch for flowers and pods.” Students put their journals away.
Everyone says “born, grow, reproduce, die” with the hand motions. Say, “Today you show what you know about a life cycle. You will draw one and label it.”
segments.teacherNotes: Safety: beans and bag contents are never tasted. Students wash hands after touching the bags, and tell you about any mold; do not open moldy bags. Beans are a choking risk for young children, so the bags stay sealed. Keep this short; the drawing needs the time. This is the last bean check. After class, plant each sprouted bean in a cup of soil on the windowsill, so the class can keep watching for flowers and pods.

segments.title: How the drawing is scored
segments.description:
Show a chart with two columns, My stages and My words, and four rows: Excellent, Good, Developing, Beginning. Read each row aloud. Say that spelling does not count.
Model with the chicken, which is not one of today’s choices. Draw an egg in a nest and write the label “egg” under it.
Ask, “What comes next? Is my drawing in order so far?”
Point to the chart and say, “You will check your own drawing against these words before you hand it in.”
segments.teacherNotes:
The rubric scores two rows, each on its own.
Stages and order. Excellent (4 points): every stage is drawn, all in the correct order. Good (3 points): one stage is missing or in the wrong place. Developing (2 points): two stages are missing or in the wrong place. Beginning (1 point): three or more stages are missing or in the wrong place.
Stage labels. Excellent (4 points): every stage has a label that names it correctly. Good (3 points): one stage has a missing or wrong label. Developing (2 points): two stages have missing or wrong labels. Beginning (1 point): three or more stages have missing or wrong labels.
Spelling does not count: a word that can be read, such as “krisalis”, is correct. A stage that is not drawn counts as a missing label. A drawing earns up to 8 points.
The student chart shows the same rows in kid words, with no points. My stages: all my stages, in order / one stage missing or in the wrong place / two stages missing or in the wrong place / three or more. My words: every stage has the right word / one word missing or wrong / two words missing or wrong / three or more.
Expected: students say “chick” comes next. Do not finish the model; students must not copy it.

segments.title: Choose a life cycle and plan it
segments.description:
Each student chooses the bean, the butterfly or the frog.
They take the picture cards for that cycle and lay them in order on their desk.
They take a word bank strip for their cycle and read the words quietly to a partner.
Students then touch each card in order, saying the stage name aloud.
segments.teacherNotes:
Before class, take down the rows of cards posted on the board last time, so the order is not on display. Give each student a mixed-up set of cards for the cycle they choose.
Word banks, one per strip, with the words in mixed order:
Butterfly: chrysalis, egg, butterfly, caterpillar.
Frog: froglet, egg, adult frog, tadpole.
Bean: seedling, seed, new seeds in a pod, sprout, adult plant. Accept “pod” for the last bean stage.
Students may use their own cards and word bank while planning and drawing. Do not check or fix the order of their cards. Children may switch cycles before they start drawing.

segments.title: Draw and label one life cycle
segments.description:
Each student draws every stage of their chosen life cycle in order on one sheet.
Under each stage they write the correct label from the word bank.
Walk around and say, “Tell me about your drawing,” without giving answers.
Students who finish early add color to their stages.
segments.teacherNotes: This is the only graded work in the unit, and it is 100% of the unit grade. Do not score while students draw: collect the drawings and score them after class with the rubric. Give no hints about answers; students use only their word bank and cards. Safety: pencils and crayons only; no scissors or glue. Common mistakes: stages out of order, and a missing chrysalis or froglet. Spelling does not count: accept any label that can be read.

segments.title: Check with the rubric and share
segments.description:
Students read the four rubric rows and decide which words fit their drawing.
They touch each stage and its label, checking the order, and fix anything they want to change.
Students hand in their drawings and return their bean bags to the window.
Students end by whispering the stages of their chosen cycle in order.
segments.teacherNotes: Students only check their work. You decide the levels after class. Expected: some children find a missing label or a stage in the wrong place. Spelling does not count, so do not send them to fix spelling. Collect all drawings, including unfinished ones, so every student can be scored. Bags go back to the window sealed.

keyIdeas: A life cycle drawing shows every stage of one living thing in the right order, from the beginning to the adult that starts the cycle again.
A label is a word that names a stage. A good label uses the correct word, such as chrysalis or tadpole.
Students choose one life cycle (the bean, the butterfly or the frog) and draw and label its stages using the picture cards and word bank as a guide.

The drawing is scored for two things: the stages are in the right order, and each stage has the correct label. Each one gets its own level: Excellent, Good, Developing or Beginning. Spelling does not count.

study.overview: Today you drew one life cycle and labeled each stage. A life cycle shows how a living thing is born, grows, reproduces and dies. You chose the bean, the butterfly or the frog. This guide helps you remember what a good life cycle drawing needs, and how your drawing is checked.

points.heading: What a life cycle drawing shows
points.explanation: A life cycle drawing shows every stage of one living thing in the right order. It starts at the beginning and goes all the way to the adult that starts the cycle again. Example: a frog drawing has four stages in order: egg, tadpole, froglet, adult frog. If you leave out the froglet, your drawing is missing a stage. Use the picture cards to help you put the stages in order.

points.heading: Labels use the correct word
points.explanation: A label is a word that names a stage. A good label uses the correct word. Write each label under its stage. Example: for a butterfly, the labels are egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly. The word bank strip helps you spell them. Readable spelling is fine. Be careful not to skip the chrysalis, because it is easy to forget.

points.heading: How your drawing is scored
points.explanation: Your drawing gets two levels: one for your stages and one for your labels. Each level is Excellent, Good, Developing or Beginning. For stages, Excellent means every stage is drawn in the correct order. Good means one stage is missing or in the wrong place. Developing means two stages are, and Beginning means three or more are. For labels, Excellent means every stage has the right word. Good means one word is missing or wrong. Developing means two words are, and Beginning means three or more are. Spelling does not count. Before you hand in a drawing, touch each stage and its label in order and check it against these words.

points.heading: What all living things share
points.explanation: The bean, the butterfly and the frog are all living things, so they share the same big pattern: born, grow, reproduce, die. You said these words with hand motions at the start of class. Example: a bean starts as a seed and a butterfly starts as an egg. Both grow and change, and both become adults that start the cycle again. Try whispering the stages of your chosen life cycle in order to help you remember them.
